transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-12-05
- Start: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~42 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leo (Redwood SE), Rajiv (CTO - StellarBay), Elena (Head of Platform), Marcus (Eng Lead), Priya (Security)

Summary: quick discovery to understand how fast StellarBay can get to a first call using Redwood API credits, what constraints push them to Dedicated or Private, and what security gating items they need for procurement.

00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving the time. I'm Maya, account lead for Redwood.
00:08 Rajiv Menon: Hey Maya, hi team. Yeah, quick morning for us. We wanted to figure out how fast we can get a feature live — like from sign-up to first token call — and then what the path looks like for us to move from prototype to production.
00:22 Leo Park: Great. I can cover the TTFT and the quickstart mechanics and then we can walk through hosting options and security considerations. Just to set expectations, TTFT for a simple text-generation call is usually under an hour for devs with our quickstart and credits; more like days if you want dedicated benchmarking or private deployment.
00:40 Elena Cruz: Under an hour sounds almost too good to be true. Do you actually mean first successful request, like a single curl or SDK call?
00:48 Leo Park: Yes a single curl or SDK call. We provide a sandbox API key and SDKs. Walkthrough: sign up -> create API key -> run sample curl -> you get streaming token response. If you're using our JS/Go SDKs it's basically sample repo clone and one line to run.
01:05 Marcus Li: What's the catch — latency and cost? If we prototype on hosted and then later switch to dedicated, does that change token behavior or model versions?
01:13 Maya Chen: Good question. Hosted is the fastest to value — same models, but dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and predictable throughput. Model versions can be pinned either way, but if you move to dedicated we can pin to a quantized variant that reduces cost. There may be small perf differences due to hardware and quantization, but behavior is functionally the same.
01:34 Priya Sharma: From security, our procurement needs SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and KMS wrapping for customer keys for PII. How does Redwood handle that?
01:44 Leo Park: We do SOC2 and can provide the report. For keys we support bring-your-own-key via KMS integrations for Private deployments; for Hosted customers we have managed encryption at rest and in transit, and a customer-specific key option for Dedicated in some contracts. For VPC/private we can do a private control plane and HSM integrations — that typically pushes timeline out a few weeks depending on network setup.
02:10 Rajiv Menon: Timeline is key. We have a Q1 launch target for a recommendation feature. Ideally, we'd like to have a pilot with real traffic by mid-January. Is that realistic?
02:20 Maya Chen: If mid-Jan is the goal, a PLG self-serve quickstart using hosted + credits now for devs to iterate is the recommended path. We can enable credits and a sandbox in minutes, you get to first call within an hour, and then run a pilot on hosted. If you need Dedicated or Private for compliance, that often requires procurement lead time — usually 4–8 weeks after contract.
02:40 Elena Cruz: Let's dig into volume. Our expected QPS for the pilot is 30 qps with spikes to 120 qps for 10–15 minutes during batch runs. Payloads are typically short — 30–80 tokens input, 50–200 tokens output for the generator. How does Redwood handle burst and KV cache with those patterns?
02:59 Leo Park: Good call. Our runtime supports burst capacity and continuous batching. For short prompts we optimize kernels and can do batching every few ms to preserve latency. For pilot levels like 30 qps, hosted will usually handle that without issue; if you need guaranteed headroom and isolation we recommend Dedicated with reserved GPUs and configurable autoscale/burst. KV cache is automatic for chatting style workloads; it can reduce compute for repeated prefixes.
03:22 Marcus Li: Any previses on per-call cost for those token sizes? Ballpark.
03:27 Maya Chen: Ballpark depends on model family and quantization. On hosted, estimates for a 200-token response on an open model variant might be $0.002–0.006 per call; with dedicated and quantized weights we can push unit costs lower but you'd need committed usage. We can share a costing sheet tailored to your traffic.
03:45 Rajiv Menon: Who else do you see in the market doing similar? We already use OpenAI for some prototypes.
03:50 Maya Chen: Many customers start with OpenAI, Anthropic, or open models. Redwood positions as a production-ready inference layer with unified runtime for hosted/dedicated/private. If your blocker is compliance or latency predictability, Dedicated or Private often wins there.
04:05 Priya Sharma: Can you describe the private deployment in more detail — like on-prem vs VPC? We are leaning to keep PII inside our VPC.
04:13 Leo Park: Sure. We have two private modes. VPC-private — the customer runs data-plane in a VPC with a private control plane; network peering is needed. On-prem is for air-gapped setups; that’s heavier and takes more integration. Both support KMS and auditing, and we provide an install runbook. Most customers go VPC-first to retain cloud benefits while keeping data on their network.
04:36 Elena Cruz: What about rollouts — can we canary model changes and fallback if a newer model regresses?
04:42 Leo Park: Yes, Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automated fallback policies. We also integrate evals so you can bind prompt sets and monitor quality regressions and get alerts.
04:55 Rajiv Menon: If we start with hosted for prototyping, what are the common gotchas when later moving to Dedicated?
05:02 Maya Chen: Main gotchas: differences in latency characteristics if you change instance type, tokenization differences for some model forks, and packaging model variants for quantization. We run compatibility tests during migration and recommend a small benchmarking effort before switching production traffic.
05:16 Marcus Li: Can you run a benchmark against our typical payloads? We can provide a corpus.
05:20 Leo Park: Absolutely. We usually do a 2–4 hour benchmark run under controlled QPS to collect P95/P99 latencies and throughput. We'll need sample payloads, approximate concurrency, and target sequence lengths.
05:32 Elena Cruz: For the quickstart, will developer keys be rate-limited? How do you avoid noisy neighbors in hosted?
05:38 Leo Park: For free credits and sandbox keys there are soft rate limits to keep things stable, but you can request higher quotas for pilot. For production hosted customers we have rate-limiting policies per account and per-route; Dedicated gives you isolation.
05:52 Priya Sharma: Can Redwood sign an NDA or do we need to wait for procurement? Also curious about contractual SLOs for hosted.
05:59 Maya Chen: We can do an NDA quickly. Hosted SLOs vary by plan; dedicated comes with stronger SLAs. Procurement normally wants SOC2 report + security questionnaire — we'll send you the security pack.
06:12 Rajiv Menon: Okay let's talk next steps then.
06:15 Maya Chen: Proposed next steps: enable 60k credits for your sandbox, share the quickstart repo link, Leo will schedule the benchmark run, and Priya we will share the SOC2 and KMS docs.
06:26 Elena Cruz: Sounds good. Also want to ask about pricing granularity — do you price per-token only or are there model-hour/instance charges for Dedicated?
06:34 Maya Chen: Hosted is per-token. Dedicated is a mix: reserved capacity (monthly/annual) for GPUs plus a smaller per-request compute charge for usage above baseline. We'll send a sample committed contract illustration.
06:46 Marcus Li: Quick technical nit — do you support OpenTelemetry tracing or something for request-level tracing?
06:52 Leo Park: Yes we have tracing hooks and per-request tracing integration with OpenTelemetry and we surface token-level cost/latency in the Console, plus per-route dashboards.
07:00 Speaker 3: (muffled) how do I…
07:02 Maya Chen: (laughs) sorry, who was that?
07:04 Marcus Li: That was our intern — ignore, he was trying to share a doc link.
07:08 Rajiv Menon: On the credits — will those be single-use or multiple developers can draw from the same bucket?
07:13 Maya Chen: We can provision an account-level credit pool so multiple devs can use it. Also can set per-key limits.
07:18 Priya Sharma: Last question from compliance: do you retain request logs and for how long? And can we request deletion?
07:25 Leo Park: For Hosted customers we store logs for X days by default (we'll provide exact retention in the security doc) and we support log redaction for PII. Dedicated/Private options can route logs to your storage for retention policy control, and deletion requests follow our data retention policy — we'll include that detail.
07:45 Maya Chen: OK let's recap: action items — I will send the pricing/hosting deck and enable credits; Leo will coordinate the benchmark; Elena will share traffic profile and Marcus will prepare payloads. We'll aim to reconvene after the benchmark run.
08:04 Rajiv Menon: Great. Thanks all — I think the mid-Jan pilot is doable if procurement and networking line up.
08:11 Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the links and the calendar invite.

Notes about audio/transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and filler words. Some product names transcribed slightly off (e.g. "KV cache" heard as "K-V cake" at 03:02), but content otherwise intact.
